Fact.Name: Form 8606 line 11 — nontaxable portion of the Roth conversion (line 8 × line 10)
Fact.Description: Line 8 x the line-10 ratio, the printed multiplication verbatim: Round(line 8 x /form8606Line10Thousandths / 1000), capped by LesserOf at line 8 itself. WHY THE PRINTED RATIO AND NOT A FULL-PRECISION RECOMPUTATION. Recomputing the ratio in place, as line 8 x line 5 / line 9, is equally compliant - the form says "rounded to AT LEAST 3 places" - and it does not FOOT: this dictionary also prints line 10, and it prints it at exactly three decimals through /form8606Line10Thousandths, so a reader who does the printed arithmetic - line 8 times the line 10 that is actually on the page - got a different number from the line 11 beside it. The printed line 11 is "Multiply line 8 by line 10", and line 10 is the entered decimal, so line 11 must be computed from the entered decimal. It now is. The change is bounded by the third decimal place: at most line 8 / 2000 of a dollar, rounded, and it can fall either way. The 1.000 ceiling is now applied where the form applies it, on line 10 itself (/form8606Line10Thousandths LesserOf 1000); the LesserOf against line 8 is kept as a belt-and-braces cap on the nontaxable portion, which the ceiling already guarantees. Guarded by the branch question (line 9 = 0 never divides - qa caution 1); the ratio fact carries the same zero-denominator arm independently. Whole-dollar rounded like every 8606 amount line. THE SPOUSE'S COPY FOLLOWS THE SAME RULE: /spouseForm8606NontaxableConversionPortion and /spouseForm8606NontaxableDistributionPortion multiply by her own printed ratio, /spouseForm8606Line10Thousandths, which is rounded exactly as this filer's is, so each filer's printed Part I foots to that filer's printed line 10 and identical inputs print identical lines on either copy.

Fact.Name: Form 8606 — Worksheet 1-1 situation (same-year contribution that may not be fully deductible + distribution/conversion)
Fact.Description:
The Pub 590-B "Contribution and distribution in the same year" situation requiring Worksheet 1-1 — a 2025 traditional-IRA distribution or Roth conversion PLUS a same-year traditional-IRA contribution that may not be fully deductible because of the §219(g) income limits. The income-limits signal is modeled EX-ANTE, as employer-plan coverage (iraDeduction:/iraDeductionPhaseoutApplies) MINUS the cases in which full deductibility is PROVABLE without resolving line 4b (iraDeduction:/iraDeductionProvablyNotReducedByIncomeLimits). The ex-post deduction-less-than-contribution comparison remains unusable because §219(g) MAGI contains the very taxable amount this route determines (the circularity Worksheet 1-1 exists to break — its numerator is deduction-independent); the upper-bound exclusion is NOT that comparison, because a monotone MAGI UPPER bound is computable acyclically and decides only the one direction that needs no circle. Complete-safe false when the Form 8606 intake is not claimed or the IRA-contribution writable is unanswered: a return outside that situation resolves false and takes the plain route.
DISCLOSURE (widened by the upper-bound exclusion): /iraDeductionPhaseoutApplies is itself flow-derived (a Filter over W-2 Box-13 answers) and is NOT IsComplete-guarded here — on a WS-situation return an unanswered Box 13 cascades Incomplete through this fact into lines 13/15c/18, the same cascade channel the IRA deduction itself already has; no committed scenario hits it. The upper-bound exclusion ENLARGES that surface by two orders of magnitude and the honest statement is not the one above: via iraDeduction:/iraDeductionProvablyNotReducedByIncomeLimits this fact now transitively reads the ENTIRE income side — all nine clean /totalIncome addends, /adjustmentsExcludingStudentLoanAndIra, /socialSecurityBenefits, and Schedule E's four claims gates. Any Incomplete among them cascades here. That is not merely theoretical: form4797:/form4797OrdinaryIncome REFUSES on purpose for a §1250 disposition. The RUNTIME consequence is still nil — /totalIncome reads the same addends, so such a return is already Incomplete and refuses regardless of this fact — but the channel is now the whole income side, not just Box 13, and a reader should know that before assuming this fact is complete-safe. It is not.

Fact.Name: Form 8606 line 15b - the part of line 15a attributable to qualified disaster distributions
Fact.Description: The portion of line 15a that came from qualified disaster distributions reported on Form 8915-F. ONE BOX, ONE INTAKE: Form 8606 line 15b and Form 8915-F line 18 are the same figure and each form directs the filer to enter it on the other, so this fact READS form8915F:/form8915FLine18Form8606Line15bOrZero rather than minting a second question for the same box. Subtracting it here is what stops the qualified disaster amount reaching Form 1040 line 4b twice - once through line 15c and again through Form 8915-F line 26. ATTRIBUTION. Form 8915-F is one return-level form in this dictionary, with no per-filer copy, while Form 8606 is per filer. The amount is therefore attributed to the filer who is the only one with a Form 8606: the primary takes it when the primary claims Form 8606 and the secondary does not. THE FIGURE IS THE FILER'S OWN PRO-RATA COMPUTATION, not a copy of a single box. i8606 Line 15b: with NO qualified disaster distributions enter -0-; with ALL distributions qualified disaster distributions enter line 15a itself; otherwise multiply line 15a by a fraction whose numerator is the total qualified disaster distributions and whose denominator is Form 8606 line 7. Its Example 1 is $30,000 on line 15a times $22,000 / $33,000 = $20,000 on line 15b and on Form 8915-F line 18. This dictionary does NOT compute that fraction - it has no per-distribution qualified disaster amount to be its numerator - so the filer supplies the result, and the screen must carry the rule. A RESIDUE THAT FOLLOWS AND IS NOT GUARDED: the fraction implies 15b is at most line 15a times QDD over line 7, tighter than the 15b at most 15a that /knockoutForm8606QualifiedDisasterPortionExceedsItsLine checks; in Example 1 the true bound is $20,000 against a checked bound of $30,000. When BOTH filers claim, neither takes it and /knockoutForm8606QualifiedDisasterAmountUnattributedBetweenFilers refuses the return rather than defaulting silently to the primary. 0 for every return that files no Form 8915-F.

Fact.Name: Section 408(o)(2)(B)(i)(I) — the section 219 deduction determined without regard to section 219(g) (primary filer)
Fact.Description:
Term (I) of the section 408(o)(2) nondeductible limit — what the primary filer's traditional-IRA deduction WOULD be if the section 219(g) active-participant phase-out did not exist. Structurally this is iraDeduction:/primaryFilerTraditionalIraDeduction's own body with a single operand swapped: the phased /iraDeductionLimitFromPhaseout gives way to the unphased /iraAnnualContributionLimit, which is precisely what "determined without regard to section 219(g)" means in this module's terms. Every other arm is carried over deliberately rather than simplified away, because term (I) and term (II) are subtracted from each other and must be computed on comparable terms: (a) the section 219(d)(4) denial reaches it through the contribution operand: the amount paid to an inherited IRA is taken off the contribution, so the amount allowable without regard to 219(g) excludes it, and a yes answer with that amount blank holds the limit (TAX-INTERPRETATIONS IN-336; the earlier whole-contribution zero arm was removed). The divergence witness tests/nodes/ty2025/form8606/ceiling-inherited-ira-zeroes-the-limit-knockout answers the amount; (b) both the compensation operand and contribution operand match the shipping deduction: the compensation operand is the section 219(c) KBH-adjusted /primaryFilerIraCompensationForDeductionLimit, not the plain compensation fact, for the same comparable-terms reason; and the contribution is /primaryFilerTraditionalIraContributionsNetOfReturnedContributionAndEndowmentLifeInsurance, which also leaves out a contribution returned by the due date (Form 8606 line 1: do not include contributions returned to you with the related earnings). Section 408(o) disregards section 219(g), not the section 219(d)(3) denial of an endowment-contract life-insurance premium, so retaining the raw contribution there would fabricate basis; (c) the IsComplete guard on the contribution intake, and the $0 fallthrough behind it, keep this fact COMPLETE for every filer. That matters structurally, not just cosmetically: /primaryFilerTraditionalIraContributions is a bare Writable Dollar with no Limit and no Placeholder that an 8606 filer need never touch — only 12 of this module's 28 committed node-test fixtures answer it — and an unguarded read would make this fact, the ceiling and the knockout all Incomplete for the other 16, which includes both cleanroom-verified cases. Because this body's dependency cone is a SUBSET of the shipping deduction's (which must resolve everywhere, feeding Schedule 1 line 20 and so AGI), completeness is inherited by construction. ROUNDING: the Round mirrors the deduction's own, so that term (I) minus term (II) telescopes cent-exactly. Without it a non-whole compensation figure would leave a spurious dollar of ceiling behind.
THE COMPENSATION LEG IS NET OF THE ALLOWED SECTION 501(c)(18) DEDUCTION (iraDeduction:/primaryFilerIraCompensationLess501c18), as the deduction's own ceiling is: section 219(b)(1) caps all section 219 deductions together at the lesser of the deductible amount and compensation, and the allowed section 501(c)(18) deduction comes off that lesser amount (TAX-INTERPRETATIONS IN-301; 26 U.S.C. 219, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section219&num=0&edition=2024). Term (I) is then the section 4973 allowable amount the package calls U (IN-305), so term (I) minus term (II) stays comparable. FED-1040-IRADED-501C18-012; FED-1040-IRADED-F8606-010.

Fact.Name: Section 131 difficulty-of-care payments excluded from gross income (primary filer)
Fact.Description: Screen "Difficulty-of-care payments you excluded from income", in the Form 8606 Part I group. QUESTION: "In 2025, did you exclude any qualified foster care payments from your income because they were difficulty-of-care payments? Enter the total amount you excluded." HELP: a difficulty-of-care payment is a qualified foster care payment a state, a political subdivision or a placement agency pays you for caring in your own home for a qualifying individual with a physical, mental or emotional handicap; section 131 keeps it out of gross income. Because it is excluded it is not compensation, so it supports no deductible IRA contribution — but section 408(o)(5) lets you elect to raise your nondeductible limit by it, capped at the amount by which the year's section 219(b) IRA contribution limit exceeds the compensation you did include in income (26 U.S.C. 408, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section408&num=0&edition=2024). Entering an amount here IS that election: the statute provides no separate election form, and the election can only ever raise the limit, never lower it. ASKED WHEN the filer opens the Form 8606 Part I intake (/writableHasForm8606 answered yes). UNANSWERED: treated as $0 — no increase is taken, the ceiling is the plain section 408(o)(2) limit, and nothing on the return goes blank or is refused. VALIDATION: dollars and cents, minimum $0, no maximum — the statutory lesser-of caps the increase itself, so a filer who excluded more than the increase can absorb should still enter the whole excluded amount. FEEDS /form8606DifficultyOfCareLimitIncrease, and through it the section 408(o)(2) ceiling and the line 1 consistency refusal. Not printed on Form 8606 or on any other form; it changes only how much of line 1 this return will accept.

Fact.Name: Section 408(o)(5) increase to the nondeductible limit (primary filer)
Fact.Description: The elective increase section 408(o)(5) allows a filer who excluded a section 131 difficulty-of-care payment: the LESSER of the excluded amount and the excess of the section 219(b) deductible amount over the compensation includible in the filer's gross income, floored at $0 because the statute frames the first operand as an excess and an excess is never negative. THE TRIGGER IS COMPENSATION BELOW THE SECTION 219(b) AMOUNT, not compensation of zero: a caregiver with some includible wages and a large excluded payment still has a positive excess, and the increase is the smaller of the two figures. THE OPERANDS ARE THIS DICTIONARY'S OWN. The section 219(b) deductible amount is the flat $7,000/$8,000 figure with the section 219(b)(5)(B) catch-up (see below; it is not reduced by the section 501(c)(18) deduction); the includible compensation is iraDeduction:/primaryFilerIraCompensation, the single-earner compensation fact this dictionary uses wherever section 219 says "compensation includible in the individual's gross income". Deliberately NOT the section 219(c) KBH-adjusted /primaryFilerIraCompensationForDeductionLimit: section 408(o)(5)(B) asks what THIS individual included, and a spouse's earnings are not that. COMPLETE-SAFE on a real "the filer answered" predicate rather than on the always-true IsComplete of a complete-safe fact: the guard is IsComplete of the intake itself, and the fallthrough is $0, so this fact resolves for every return and the ceiling stays Complete. NOT COVERED: the employer-plan half of the same SECURE Act rule. Section 408(o)(5) reaches the IRA nondeductible limit and nothing else, which is the only limit this module enforces. THE DEDUCTIBLE AMOUNT IS THE FLAT SECTION 219(b)(5) FIGURE. Section 408(o)(5)(A) measures from "the deductible amount in effect for the taxable year" under section 219(b) (26 U.S.C. 408, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section408&num=0&edition=2024): $7,000, or $8,000 with the catch-up (iraDeduction:/iraAnnualContributionLimitStandard or /iraAnnualContributionLimitCatchUp), NOT /iraAnnualContributionLimit, which is net of the section 501(c)(18) deduction (FED-1040-IRADED-F8606-010). Under IN-304 as amended the increase raises only the compensation side of Form 8606 line 1, where that side is capped at the deductible amount (/form8606NondeductibleContributionCeiling and its spouse twin; 26 U.S.C. 408, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section408&num=0&edition=2024).

Fact.Name: Form 8606 line 1 — repayment of a qualified reservist distribution (primary filer)
Fact.Description: Screen "Repayment of a qualified reservist distribution", in the Form 8606 Part I group. QUESTION: "Is any part of the amount on Form 8606 line 1 a repayment of a qualified reservist distribution? Enter the repayment amount." HELP: a qualified reservist distribution is one you took from an IRA or from elective deferrals while ordered or called to active duty for more than 179 days or for an indefinite period, after 11 September 2001. You may repay it to an IRA at any time in the 2-year period beginning the day after the active-duty period ends, and section 72(t)(2)(G)(ii) says the dollar limits that normally apply to IRA contributions do not apply to that repayment and that no deduction is allowed for it (26 U.S.C. 72, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section72&num=0&edition=2024). The Form 8606 instructions therefore tell you to include the repayment on line 1 (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i8606.pdf, page 9). DO NOT also report this repayment as a traditional IRA contribution in the IRA deduction questions: no deduction is allowed for it, and reporting it there would claim one. ASKED WHEN the filer opens the Form 8606 Part I intake (/writableHasForm8606 answered yes). UNANSWERED: treated as $0, so the section 408(o)(2) ceiling is unchanged and nothing on the return goes blank or is refused. VALIDATION: dollars and cents, minimum $0, no maximum — the statute exempts the repayment from the dollar limits outright, and the repayment cannot exceed the distribution, a lifetime figure this single-year graph does not carry. FEEDS /form8606QualifiedReservistRepayment, and through it the section 408(o)(2) ceiling and the line 1 consistency refusal. Not printed as a line of its own; it is part of the line 1 the filer already attested.

Fact.Name: Qualified reservist repayment included in Form 8606 line 1 (primary filer)
Fact.Description: The complete-safe reading of the reservist-repayment intake: the amount answered, else $0. It enters the section 408(o)(2) ceiling as an increase because section 72(t)(2)(G)(ii) puts the repayment outside the dollar limitations on IRA contributions altogether — expressing that exemption as an increase to the ceiling is what keeps the line 1 the instructions require from being refused, without letting the repayment enlarge the limit for any other contribution. NO DEDUCTION FOLLOWS IT. The same clause forbids a deduction for the repayment, so this fact does not enter the IRA deduction chain and the intake's own screen tells the filer not to report the repayment as a traditional IRA contribution. The guard is IsComplete of the intake itself, a genuine "the filer answered" predicate, and the fallthrough is $0, so the ceiling stays Complete for every return.

Fact.Name: Form 8606 line 1 — the section 408(o)(2) nondeductible limit (primary filer)
Fact.Description:
The most a filer may designate as a nondeductible contribution, enforced as a CONSISTENCY REFUSAL and never as a cap (see the knockout below; nothing in the basis chain reads this fact, and line 1 must keep its out-degree of 0). THE FORMULA. Section 408(o)(2)(B) defines the limit as term (I) minus term (II), plus clause (ii)'s increase for an amount the filer "elects not to deduct". The last two terms TELESCOPE: elected-not-to-deduct is by definition the allowable amount minus the amount actually deducted, so limit = term (I) minus the amount ACTUALLY deducted on Schedule 1 line 20, which for this filer is the ordinary deduction plus the section 219(f)(6) deemed amount (iraDeduction:/primaryFilerSection219f6PriorYearExcessDeduction), because i8606's Line 1 subtracts worksheet line 12, and line 12 deducts from line 11 including the bridge amount (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i5329.pdf, page 6; https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i8606.pdf, page 9). So term (I) is taken together with the bridge amount (iraDeduction:/primaryFilerSection219f6BridgeAmount), the smaller of Form 5329 line 10 and line 9 less lines 11 and 12; the part of it the phased room does not deduct becomes line 1 basis (package meaning Q11, TAX-INTERPRETATIONS IN-309, provisional). The bridge is never more than the unphased room left after the contribution, so term (I) plus the bridge is still the smaller of worksheet lines 10 and 11. $0 with no prior-year excess. The dependency this fact subtracts IS that deducted amount by construction: iraDeduction:/primaryFilerTraditionalIraDeduction is already clamped by iraDeduction:/primaryFilerElectedTraditionalIraDeductionAmount, so the ceiling rises by the elected-away amount without needing a term of its own. Statute, form instruction and publication worksheet are one formula here: i8606's Line 1 says to subtract the worksheet's deduction line "(or the amount you chose to deduct on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 20, if less) from the smaller of line 10 or line 11", and Pub 590-A Worksheet 1-2 prints the same arithmetic as its line 8 and names the result as the value of Form 8606 line 1 itself. NON-NEGATIVE by the GreaterOf floor: term (II) cannot exceed term (I) on this dictionary's own facts (the deduction's phased limit is bounded by the unphased one), so the floor is defensive rather than statutory — the eitc.xml /eitcEarnedIncomeBase precedent. THE QUALIFIED RESERVIST REPAYMENT (/form8606QualifiedReservistRepayment, section 72(t)(2)(G)(ii), which exempts it from the dollar limitations on IRA contributions outright, and which i8606's Line 1 instruction tells the filer to include on line 1) IS ADDED AFTER THAT FLOOR. The section 408(o)(5) increase (/form8606DifficultyOfCareLimitIncrease) is not: it raises the compensation side inside the LesserOf, capped at the flat deductible amount (IN-304 as amended, below). Both are complete-safe and resolve $0 for a filer who answers neither intake. ZERO IS THE FALLTHROUGH, NOT AN ENFORCED LIMIT. For a filer with no current-year IRA contribution on record this resolves 0, because both terms are 0. Read alone that looks like a ceiling of zero refusing everything; it is not, because the knockout carries its own IsComplete conjunct on the same intake and stays silent for exactly that population. The two facts must be read together. SEQUENCING (and why the ceiling can read the deduction at all): the printed order is sequential — the IRA Deduction Worksheet runs on coverage, filing status, MAGI, compensation and contributions, and no printed step in it asks for Form 8606 line 1. Line 1 falls out afterwards. A sibling fact that needed the same deduction information from INSIDE the income chain had to gate on the contribution intake instead, because there the read closes a cycle; that workaround is correct there and must not be copied here. This fact sits OUTSIDE that chain — nothing downstream of it feeds AGI — so it may read the deduction itself, which is what makes the FULL statutory limit expressible rather than a weaker term-(I)-only bound. NOT COVERED: an attestation BELOW the printed result. That forfeits basis, runs against the filer's own interest, and this fact does not answer it.
IN-304 AS AMENDED (TAX-INTERPRETATIONS): line 1 is the smaller of the compensation side and the contributions, minus the deduction actually taken, plus any qualified reservist repayment (Instructions for Form 8606 (2025), Line 1, https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i8606.pdf, page 9). The section 408(o)(5) increase (/form8606DifficultyOfCareLimitIncrease) raises only the compensation side, which never exceeds the deductible amount: an IRA accepts no more than "the amount in effect for such taxable year under section 219(b)(1)(A)" (26 U.S.C. 408, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section408&num=0&edition=2024) and Pub. 590-A allows the increase "but not above the $7,000 IRA deductible amount" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p590a.pdf, page 16). So the increase sits inside the compensation side, capped at the flat deductible amount. Contributions within the section 219 allowable amount become nondeductible only by an election not to deduct them (IRC 408(o)(2)(B)(ii)), which the deduction subtracted here already reflects. When Roth contributions use up the excise room the section 219(f)(6) deduction can exceed the bridge (TAX-INTERPRETATIONS IN-309 amendment); the excess was never in line 11, so only the part held inside the bridge, net of the answered closed-year amount (iraDeduction:/primaryFilerSection219f6DeductionWithinBridgeAmount), comes off here, less the part of it a designation elects not to deduct (iraDeduction:/primaryFilerSection219f6DeductionElectedNotToDeduct, so the amount actually deducted is what is subtracted); the knockout below compares a designation with the starting amount itself (FED-1040-IRADED-F6ROTHCAP-039, ira-pilot gate D1 r3).

Fact.Name: Form 8606 line 1, the smaller of the compensation side and the contributions side (primary filer)
Fact.Description: The amount Form 8606 line 1 starts from, before the deduction taken is subtracted: "the smaller of line 10 or line 11 of the worksheet" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i8606.pdf, page 9), with the section 408(o)(5) increase on the compensation side and that side capped at the flat deductible amount (TAX-INTERPRETATIONS IN-304 as amended), and the section 219(f)(6) bridge amount on both sides (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i5329.pdf, page 6). Read by /form8606NondeductibleContributionCeiling and by iraDeduction's deduction, where a Form 8606 line 1 designation acts as the section 408(o)(2)(B)(ii) election (obligation IRA-026, reconciliation finding).

Fact.Name: Knockout: Form 8606 line 1 exceeds the section 408(o)(2) nondeductible limit
Fact.Description: Section 408(o)(2)(A) states the prohibition flatly — designated nondeductible contributions "shall not exceed the nondeductible limit for such taxable year". Nothing in this graph enforced it, so a filer could contribute 7,000, deduct 7,000, and then designate 3,000 of it nondeductible. That is not a harmless over-statement: line 1 enters the basis chain through /form8606Line3, so an over-stated line 1 UNDER-taxes a distribution this year and in every later year the basis carries forward. A REFUSAL, NOT A CAP, and the choice is forced rather than stylistic: capping line 1 means line 1 reads the ceiling, which closes the cycle. This is the user-input-contradiction guard class — the same shape as the two sibling knockouts one screen up. THE IsComplete CONJUNCT SELECTS THE COMPARISON; the fallthrough is not silence. With the contribution intake answered the designation is compared to the ceiling above. With it unanswered the contribution-dependent term of the ceiling is unknown, and the second arm refuses a line 1 above the two terms that need no contribution on record: the qualified reservist repayment (/form8606QualifiedReservistRepayment), which i8606 tells the filer to include on line 1 and which section 72(t)(2)(G)(ii) puts outside the dollar limits, and the section 408(o)(5) increase (/form8606DifficultyOfCareLimitIncrease). A line 1 made of those amounts alone is within the limit whatever the unknown term is. Neither of the other two readings is available: an unanswered contribution cannot be read as $0, because the ceiling would then be $0 and every positive line 1 would be refused on the ground that the filer contributed nothing, which is the wrong population; and reading it favourably leaves line 1 unbounded, basis inflated through /form8606Line3 and Form 1040 line 4b deflated, with nothing refusing. THE SILENCE THAT REMAINS IS EXACT, and both halves of it are deliberate. Line 1 of $0 with the intake unanswered has nothing for section 408(o)(2) to bound and stays silent; and a claiming filer who has not answered line 1 at all stays silent too, which is what the second arm's own IsComplete guard is for — the fact must not go Incomplete and contaminate the knockout aggregate. ONE REACHABLE PATH, named rather than waved away. The expectation is that the traditional-IRA contribution question is put to every filer who attests a line 1, which would make this arm unreachable through the ordinary interview; that expectation is not written down anywhere this fact can point at, so it is stated as an expectation and not as a fact. What IS reachable is the filer who answers income:/madeIraContributions No and then designates a positive line 1 anyway: the contribution intake is never put to them, and the two answers contradict each other. Refusing is the right outcome for that filer, and it is this arm that produces it. Pinned in both directions by tests/nodes/ty2025/form8606/ceiling-line1-without-the-contribution-intake-refused and by tests/nodes/ty2025/form8606/boundary-zero-basis-passthrough, which claims Form 8606, answers line 1 of $0 with no contribution intake, and asserts this fact Complete FALSE. SUBMISSION-BLOCKING ONLY, deliberately no flow:/flowIsKnockedOut membership: this is a permanent intake-consistency guard, not a scope limit, so it carries BlockSubmissionOnTrue with the scope-sidecar revisit_trigger beginning "n/a" that lint_dual_wiring's PERMANENT-NON-SCOPE-GUARD category recognises in both directions. (The four older Form 8606 knockouts predate that category and are additionally flow-wired; the discriminator, not their example, is what governs here.) It also fires when an elected deduction amount and a Form 8606 line 1 entry are both given and they disagree by $1 or more: an elected deduction and a designation must agree, or the return cannot tell which the filer meant (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i8606.pdf, page 9; IRC 408(o)(2)(B)(ii), 26 U.S.C. 408, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section408&num=0&edition=2024; obligation IRA-026, reconciliation finding; FACT-SKILL-1 2.4b). A designation with no elected amount is the election itself and sets the deduction, so it never fires this leg. It also fires on a designation given without an elected amount that is $1 or more above the most that can be designated, the line 1 starting amount (the smaller of the compensation side and the contributions side) less the section 219(f)(6) part of line 20 (TAX-INTERPRETATIONS IN-331; obligation IRA-026, reconciliation finding).

Fact.Name: Repaid a SECURE 2.0 qualified distribution within the 3-year window (primary filer)
Fact.Description: Screen "Repayments of special IRA distributions", in the Form 8606 group. QUESTION: "Did you repay, within the 3-year repayment period, any part of a qualified birth or adoption distribution, emergency personal expense distribution, domestic abuse distribution or terminal illness distribution that you are reporting on your 2025 Form 8606 - on line 7 (traditional IRA distributions) or on line 19 (Roth IRA distributions)?" ANSWER NO if the distribution you repaid was reported on an EARLIER year's Form 8606: both printed worksheets are tied to this year's form and stop at their line 3 for you, and the remedy is an amended return for the year of the distribution, which worksheet line 5's own note describes. HELP: these four distribution types can be paid back to an IRA within three years, and the repayment reduces the taxable amount the IRS expects on your return. The Form 8606 instructions give each of them a worksheet - the 2025 Line 15c Worksheet for traditional IRA distributions (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i8606.pdf, page 12) and the 2025 Line 25c Worksheet for Roth IRA distributions (lines 998 onward). ASKED WHEN the filer reports a traditional IRA distribution on Form 8606 line 7 or a nonqualified Roth distribution on line 19; asked of every such filer, because a repayment is invisible to every other answer on the return. UNANSWERED or NO: nothing changes; Form 8606 line 15c stays line 15a minus line 15b and line 25c stays line 25a, which is correct for a filer with no repayment. YES: the return is REFUSED, because this product does not yet compute either worksheet and filing without them OVER-STATES the tax by the repaid share. VALIDATION: yes or no. FEEDS /knockoutForm8606RepaymentWorksheetUnmodelled only; it moves no dollar.

Fact.Name: Section 131 difficulty-of-care payments excluded from gross income (secondary filer)
Fact.Description: Screen "Difficulty-of-care payments your spouse excluded from income", in the secondary filer's Form 8606 Part I group. QUESTION: "In 2025, did your spouse exclude any qualified foster care payments from income because they were difficulty-of-care payments? Enter the total amount excluded." HELP: a difficulty-of-care payment is a qualified foster care payment a state, a political subdivision or a placement agency pays for caring in the caregiver's own home for a qualifying individual with a physical, mental or emotional handicap; section 131 keeps it out of gross income. Because it is excluded it is not compensation, so it supports no deductible IRA contribution — but section 408(o)(5) lets your spouse elect to raise her own nondeductible limit by it, capped at the amount by which the year's section 219(b) IRA contribution limit exceeds the compensation she did include in income (26 U.S.C. 408, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section408&num=0&edition=2024). Entering an amount here IS that election. Section 219(f)(2) computes each spouse's limit separately, so this answer never affects the primary filer's ceiling. ASKED WHEN the secondary filer opens her own Form 8606 Part I intake (/writableSpouseHasForm8606 answered yes). UNANSWERED: treated as $0 — no increase, the plain section 408(o)(2) limit, nothing blank and nothing refused. VALIDATION: dollars and cents, minimum $0, no maximum. FEEDS /spouseForm8606DifficultyOfCareLimitIncrease and, through it, the secondary filer's ceiling and her line 1 consistency refusal. Not printed on Form 8606 or on any other form.

THE DEDUCTIBLE AMOUNT IS THE FLAT SECTION 219(b)(5) FIGURE. Section 408(o)(5)(A) measures from "the deductible amount in effect for the taxable year" under section 219(b) (26 U.S.C. 408, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section408&num=0&edition=2024): $7,000, or $8,000 with the catch-up (iraDeduction:/iraAnnualContributionLimitStandard or /iraAnnualContributionLimitCatchUp), NOT /spouseIraAnnualContributionLimit, which is net of the section 501(c)(18) deduction (FED-1040-IRADED-F8606-010). Fact.Name: Spouse Form 8606 line 1 — repayment of a qualified reservist distribution (secondary filer)
Fact.Description: Screen "Repayment of a qualified reservist distribution (spouse)", in the secondary filer's Form 8606 Part I group. QUESTION: "Is any part of the amount on your spouse's Form 8606 line 1 a repayment of a qualified reservist distribution? Enter the repayment amount." HELP: a qualified reservist distribution is one taken from an IRA or from elective deferrals while ordered or called to active duty for more than 179 days or for an indefinite period, after 11 September 2001. It may be repaid to an IRA at any time in the 2-year period beginning the day after the active-duty period ends, and section 72(t)(2)(G)(ii) says the dollar limits that normally apply to IRA contributions do not apply to that repayment and that no deduction is allowed for it (26 U.S.C. 72, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section72&num=0&edition=2024). The Form 8606 instructions therefore tell the filer to include the repayment on line 1 (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i8606.pdf, page 9). DO NOT also report this repayment as one of the spouse's traditional IRA contributions in the IRA deduction questions: no deduction is allowed for it. ASKED WHEN the secondary filer opens her own Form 8606 Part I intake (/writableSpouseHasForm8606 answered yes). UNANSWERED: treated as $0, ceiling unchanged, nothing blank and nothing refused. VALIDATION: dollars and cents, minimum $0, no maximum. FEEDS /spouseForm8606QualifiedReservistRepayment and, through it, the secondary filer's ceiling and her line 1 consistency refusal.

Fact.Name: Spouse Form 8606 line 1 — the section 408(o)(2) nondeductible limit (secondary filer)
Fact.Description:
The secondary filer's own section 408(o)(2) limit — term (I) minus the amount actually deducted for her on Schedule 1 line 20 (her ordinary deduction plus her own section 219(f)(6) deemed amount, iraDeduction:/secondaryFilerSection219f6PriorYearExcessDeduction; https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i8606.pdf, page 9), with term (I) taken together with her own section 219(f)(6) bridge amount (iraDeduction:/secondaryFilerSection219f6BridgeAmount; https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i5329.pdf, page 6), floored at $0. Mirror of /form8606NondeductibleContributionCeiling; the telescoping of clause (ii), the non-negativity floor, the sequencing argument and the zero-is-a-fallthrough caution are recorded once, there, and are not restated. Her section 408(o)(5) increase (/spouseForm8606DifficultyOfCareLimitIncrease) raises her compensation side, capped at the flat deductible amount, and her qualified reservist repayment (/spouseForm8606QualifiedReservistRepayment) is added after the floor, as on the primary fact.
IN-304 AS AMENDED (TAX-INTERPRETATIONS): line 1 is the smaller of the compensation side and the contributions, minus the deduction actually taken, plus any qualified reservist repayment (Instructions for Form 8606 (2025), Line 1, https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i8606.pdf, page 9). The section 408(o)(5) increase (/spouseForm8606DifficultyOfCareLimitIncrease) raises only the compensation side, which never exceeds the deductible amount: an IRA accepts no more than "the amount in effect for such taxable year under section 219(b)(1)(A)" (26 U.S.C. 408, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section408&num=0&edition=2024) and Pub. 590-A allows the increase "but not above the $7,000 IRA deductible amount" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p590a.pdf, page 16). So the increase sits inside the compensation side, capped at the flat deductible amount. Contributions within the section 219 allowable amount become nondeductible only by an election not to deduct them (IRC 408(o)(2)(B)(ii)), which the deduction subtracted here already reflects. When Roth contributions use up the excise room the section 219(f)(6) deduction can exceed the bridge (TAX-INTERPRETATIONS IN-309 amendment); the excess was never in line 11, so only the part held inside the bridge, net of the answered closed-year amount (iraDeduction:/secondaryFilerSection219f6DeductionWithinBridgeAmount), comes off here, less the part of it a designation elects not to deduct (iraDeduction:/secondaryFilerSection219f6DeductionElectedNotToDeduct, so the amount actually deducted is what is subtracted); the knockout below compares a designation with the starting amount itself (FED-1040-IRADED-F6ROTHCAP-039, ira-pilot gate D1 r3).

Same two-armed inner Switch on the secondary's contribution intake — the ceiling comparison when it is answered, and when it is not, a refusal of a spouse line 1 above her qualified reservist repayment plus her section 408(o)(5) increase, the two ceiling terms that need no contribution on record — and the same BlockSubmissionOnTrue-without-flow-membership shape, excused in both directions by the scope-sidecar's PERMANENT-NON-SCOPE-GUARD category. It also fires when an elected deduction amount and a Form 8606 line 1 entry are both given and they disagree by $1 or more: an elected deduction and a designation must agree, or the return cannot tell which the filer meant (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i8606.pdf, page 9; IRC 408(o)(2)(B)(ii), 26 U.S.C. 408, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section408&num=0&edition=2024; obligation IRA-026, reconciliation finding; FACT-SKILL-1 2.4b). A designation with no elected amount is the election itself and sets the deduction, so it never fires this leg. It also fires on a designation given without an elected amount that is $1 or more above the most that can be designated, the line 1 starting amount (the smaller of the compensation side and the contributions side) less the section 219(f)(6) part of line 20 (TAX-INTERPRETATIONS IN-331; obligation IRA-026, reconciliation finding).

Fact.Name: Form 8606 line 16 - net amount converted from traditional IRAs to Roth IRAs
Fact.Description: Part II line 16: the amount converted from traditional IRAs to Roth IRAs in 2025, which the form takes from Part I line 8 whenever Part I is completed. This names the value form8606.xml already computes inline as the minuend of /form8606ConversionTaxableAmount, so line 16 and line 18 cannot drift apart: the conversion intake when the Form 8606 intake is claimed; the Part II-only conversion (/writableForm8606PartIIOnlyConversion) when only Part II is completed (/form8606ClaimsPartIIOnly); 0 otherwise.

Fact.Name: Form 8606 line 17 - basis in the amount converted to a Roth IRA
Fact.Description: Part II line 17: the basis in the line 16 conversion, derived as line 16 minus line 18 so the printed Part II foots on BOTH computation routes. On the plain route line 18 is line 16 minus line 11, so this resolves to line 11 exactly as the form says. On the Pub 590-B Worksheet 1-1 route line 11 is left blank and line 18 is Worksheet 1-1 line 10, so this resolves to the worksheet basis allocated to the conversion; it equals Worksheet 1-1 line 8 whenever the whole distribution was converted, which is the published Rose Green configuration. Taking line 11 directly would print the plain-route number on a worksheet-route return. WHERE THIS DIVERGES FROM THE PUBLICATION, stated because the publication does not foot with itself here and a reader will otherwise take the tree for the error. Pub. 590-B says twice that Worksheet 1-1 line 8 goes on Form 8606 lines 13 AND 17 (p590b:1104-1105, :1190-1192). This fact honours line 13 and computes line 17 as line 16 minus line 18, which on the worksheet route equals WS line 8 times the CONVERTED share of the distribution - equal to WS line 8 itself only when the whole distribution was converted. On a mixed distribution-plus-conversion worksheet-route return the two lines the publication calls equal print different numbers. THE PUBLICATION IS THE ONE THAT DOES NOT FOOT: its own Note makes Form 8606 line 18 equal WS line 9 times the conversion share, and the form prints line 18 as line 16 minus line 17, so its line 13 and line 17 cannot both be WS line 8 unless the distribution was entirely converted. The reading kept here is the FORM's own arithmetic, because line 18 is the number that reaches Form 1040 line 4b while line 17 is print-only. This fact has no consumers, so no dollar moves either way. When only Part II is completed (/form8606ClaimsPartIIOnly) line 17 is $0: the Part II-only intake is for a filer with no basis, and the Line 17 instruction takes the basis from line 2 and line 1.

Fact.Name: The primary filer completes Form 8606 Part II without Part I
Fact.Description: True when the primary filer does not complete Part I (/claimsForm8606 false) and answers a Part II-only conversion (/writableForm8606PartIIOnlyConversion) above $0. Fact.Name: The secondary filer completes Form 8606 Part II without Part I
Fact.Description: The secondary filer's twin of /form8606ClaimsPartIIOnly: a joint return, the secondary filer does not complete Part I (/claimsSpouseForm8606 false) and answers a Part II-only conversion (/writableSpouseForm8606PartIIOnlyConversion) above $0. False otherwise.

Fact.Name: Form 8606 line 18 as printed - line 16 less line 17 (primary filer)
Fact.Description: The printed line 18: line 16 (/form8606Line16) less line 17 (/form8606Line17). Fact.Description:

Fact.Name: Form 8606 Part III opened (complete-safe)
Fact.Description: True when the primary filer answered Form 8606 line 19 with a POSITIVE amount, and false otherwise. The greater-than-zero conjunct is the printed entry condition, not decoration: i8606 says a filer with no amount to enter on line 19 must not complete Part III at all, so a line 19 answered at $0 is a filer who has no Part III, and reading it as one would silence /knockoutForm8606QualifiedDisasterAmountWithoutAForm8606 on a return with a positive Form 8915-F line 19. Part III is deliberately NOT gated on /claimsForm8606 - a filer whose only reportable distribution is a nonqualified Roth distribution files Part III with no Part I - so this is Part III's counterpart of that claim, and the two must not be substituted for each other.

Fact.Name: Form 8606 line 25b - the part of line 25a attributable to qualified disaster distributions
Fact.Description: The Roth twin of line 15b: the portion of line 25a that came from qualified disaster distributions reported on Form 8915-F, read from form8915F:/form8915FLine19Form8606Line25bOrZero because Form 8606 line 25b and Form 8915-F line 19 are one box that each form tells the filer to copy to the other. Subtracting it here is what stops the qualified disaster amount reaching Form 1040 line 4b twice, once through line 25c and again through Form 8915-F line 26. THE GATE IS PART III, NOT /claimsForm8606, and the asymmetry with line 15b is deliberate: the Part III chain hangs off /writableForm8606RothIraDistributions and a Roth-only filer never claims Part I, so gating this on the Part I claim would leave that filer's double count open. THE FIGURE IS THE FILER'S OWN PRO-RATA COMPUTATION: i8606's Line 25b rule is line 25a times total qualified disaster distributions over Form 8606 LINE 21 - not line 19, and not line 25a - with -0- when none is a qualified disaster distribution and line 25a itself when all are. This dictionary does not compute that fraction and the screen must carry the rule, denominator included. Attribution needs no test today because only the primary filer has a Part III; when the secondary filer's Part III is built this fact takes the same both-claim refusal line 15b already carries. 0 on every return that opens no Part III. the Roth worksheet uses direct repayment subtraction and per-filer Part III attribution; unresolved two-filer disaster attribution remains refused.

Fact.Name: Form 8606 line 25c - taxable amount of the Roth IRA distributions
Fact.Description: Line 25c = line 25a - line 25b. The form says to include a positive line 25c on Form 1040 line 4b; income:/taxableIraDistributions does that through the complete-safe wrapper /form8606Line25cOrZero. No zero floor: the form prints none on 25c, and line 25b above line 25a is refused as an input contradiction (/knockoutForm8606QualifiedDisasterPortionExceedsItsLine) rather than clamped. Incomplete whenever line 25a is, which is every return that opens no Part III. A repaid SECURE 2.0 distribution is given effect by the 2025 Line 25c Worksheet: /form8606QualifiedRothRepaymentReduction is subtracted as a second subtrahend, so this is worksheet line 4 when the worksheet applies, and a yes that leaves the worksheet repayment unanswered is refused (/knockoutForm8606RepaymentWorksheetUnmodelled).

Fact.Name: Form 8606 line 25c, zero when Part III is not answered
Fact.Description:
The complete safe wrapper of /form8606Line25c, the printed line 25c (line 25a less the line 25b qualified disaster portion this module reads from Form 8915-F line 19). Its guard is IsComplete of line 25a rather than of 25c because line 25b is complete-safe, so the two are Complete together and line 25a is the fact that says whether Part III produced a figure at all. income:/taxableIraDistributions adds this term outside its route Switch, so the taxable Roth distribution the form sends to Form 1040 line 4b reaches /totalIncome. The wrapper exists because the Part III chain is driven by /writableForm8606RothIraDistributions and is NOT gated on /claimsForm8606, so /form8606Line25a is Incomplete on every return that answers no Roth intake, and Form 1040 line 4b must stay Complete. Zero on every return that answers no Part III intake. THE ZERO IS NOT A SILENT ANSWER FOR A FILER WHO DID OPEN PART III: /knockoutForm8606PartIIIPartiallyAnswered refuses a return that reports a positive line 19 and leaves line 20, or a required line 22 or 24, blank, so the only returns this wrapper zeroes are the ones with no Part III to report and the ones the form's own skip rules send here.
Primary taxable Roth distribution export. With a positive Part III distribution and the history calculator selected, preserve the printed zero-line stop rules but propagate an otherwise incomplete line 25c to the return. Do not replace an unresolved selected history with zero. All unselected histories retain the pre-existing manual-route behavior and submission guard. A calculator selection without a distribution does not create taxable income.

Fact.Name: This Form 1099-R is a Roth IRA distribution with a box 2a amount above zero
Fact.Description: True when box 7 of this Form 1099-R carries a Roth IRA distribution code (J, Q or T, alone or in a permitted pair) and box 2a is above $0. False when either is unanswered, so an item still being entered never trips the refusal it feeds. The Form 1099-R route adds box 2a to Form 1040 line 4b, while the taxable part of a Roth IRA distribution belongs on line 4b from Form 8606 line 25c; an item this fact marks is counted on both when Part III is opened.

Fact.Name: Some Form 1099-R is a Roth IRA distribution with a box 2a amount above zero (complete-safe)
Fact.Description: True when at least one Form 1099-R item is marked by /form1099Rs/*/rothTaxableAmountBesideForm8606PartIII. Complete false over an absent or unanswered Form 1099-R collection.

Fact.Name: Knockout: a Roth IRA Form 1099-R box 2a amount beside a Form 8606 Part III
Fact.Description:
Refuses a return that opens Form 8606 Part III for either filer while a Form 1099-R carries a Roth IRA distribution code with a box 2a amount above $0. Form 1040 line 4b takes the taxable part of a Roth IRA distribution from Form 8606 line 25c, and the Form 1099-R route adds that form's box 2a to the same line, so the one distribution would be taxed twice: a $10,000 Roth distribution with $2,000 taxable on line 25c resolves line 4b at $12,000, and a Roth qualified disaster distribution carried to Form 8915-F line 19 reaches line 4b once through Form 8915-F and again through box 2a. Refusing is the taxpayer-safe answer until the Form 1099-R route leaves a Roth item to Part III.
SCREEN: "This return reports a Roth IRA distribution on Form 8606 and also on a Form 1099-R that shows a taxable amount in box 2a. The taxable part of a Roth IRA distribution is figured on Form 8606, and this product cannot yet keep the Form 1099-R amount from being counted a second time, so this return cannot be filed here."
NOT REFUSED: a Roth Form 1099-R with box 2a blank or $0, the usual payer entry for codes J and T; a traditional IRA Form 1099-R beside Part III; a Roth Form 1099-R with no Part III. Complete false on every return without both.

Fact.Description: Line 23 minus line 24, before the form's zero floor is applied.

Fact.Description: The zero that Part III lines 21, 23 and 25a floor at when the subtraction above them is zero or less. A named constant because the GreaterOf that applies the floor takes fact paths, not literals.

Fact.Name: Form 8606 primary Roth-conversion basis, floored at zero
Fact.Description: The computational form of Form 8606 line 24 for the primary filer. The declared basis in Roth conversions and rollovers is nonnegative; a negative persisted or migrated value cannot be subtracted from line 23 to inflate taxable distributions. The explicit floor is in the graph because the writable Limit validates intake but is not enforced on resolution. An unanswered basis remains Incomplete, preserving line 25a's required-input behavior.

Fact.Name: Qualified Roth IRA distributions with no Part III (primary filer, Form 1040 line 4a)
Fact.Description: ASK: "Enter the total of any Roth IRA distributions you received in 2025 that are not taxable and that you are not reporting in Part III of Form 8606." HELP: a Roth IRA distribution is not taxable, and Part III is not completed for it, when there is no amount to enter on Form 8606 line 19 after applying the line 19 instructions - typically a QUALIFIED distribution, one made after the 5-year period and after age 59 1/2, death, disability or a first-time home purchase. The instruction is verbatim: "If, after considering the items above, you don't have an amount to enter on line 19, don't complete Part III; your Roth IRA distribution(s) isn't taxable. Instead, include your total Roth IRA distribution(s) on 2025 Form 1040, 1040-SR, or 1040-NR, line 4a" (i8606, Part III, Line 19). ASKED WHEN: the filer reports any Roth IRA distribution. It is asked BESIDE line 19, not instead of it - one filer can have both a qualified distribution and a nonqualified one in the same year, and only the nonqualified one goes in Part III. UNANSWERED: read as $0 and nothing is added to line 4a, which is the pre-existing behaviour for every return; it is not refused, because a filer with no qualified Roth distribution has nothing to say here and no line of the return depends on the answer for its arithmetic. VALIDATION: Dollar, Min $0; the gross distribution, not a taxable amount. FEEDS: Form 1040 line 4a only (income:/iraDistributions), never line 4b - this money is not taxable.

Fact.Name: Qualified Roth IRA distributions with no Part III (secondary filer, Form 1040 line 4a)
Fact.Description: ASK: "Enter the total of any Roth IRA distributions your spouse received in 2025 that are not taxable." The primary filer's version of this question adds "and that you are not reporting in Part III of Form 8606"; HERS DOES NOT, because she has no Part III on this return to report anything in. HELP, ASKED WHEN, UNANSWERED posture and VALIDATION are /writableForm8606QualifiedRothDistributions's, word for word, with "you" meaning the spouse: a Roth IRA distribution is not taxable, and no Part III is completed for it, when there is no amount to enter on Form 8606 line 19 - typically a QUALIFIED distribution, made after the 5-year period and after age 59 1/2, death, disability or a first-time home purchase. WHAT THIS RETURN CANNOT REPORT FOR HER, stated on the intake so the box is not mistaken for a complete answer: a NONQUALIFIED Roth distribution of hers reaches neither Form 1040 line 4a nor line 4b, because Form 8606 Part III is built for the primary filer only, and nothing refuses it here. The narrow protection that exists is elsewhere and is not this module's: the 1099-R frontier admits distribution code Q but not J or T alone, so her nonqualified Roth Form 1099-R is refused on the way in; the unguarded state is the one where no Form 1099-R is entered for it and this box is used instead, which is why the ASK says NOT TAXABLE. FEEDS: Form 1040 line 4a only, never 4b.

Fact.Name: Roth IRA distributions the primary filer reports on Form 1040 line 4a
Fact.Description: The primary filer's gross Roth IRA distributions for line 4a: Part III line 19 (the distributions Part III computes a taxable amount for) plus the qualified distributions that have no Part III. Both terms are read complete-safe, so this is $0 on every return that answers neither. NOT A TAXABLE AMOUNT: line 4b takes /form8606Line25cOrZero, which is the Part III result alone; the qualified term never reaches 4b. This fact is why a nonqualified Roth distribution no longer arrives at line 4b with nothing on line 4a beside it, which is what the printed form and the payer's Form 1099-R both say should be there.

Fact.Name: Roth IRA distributions the secondary filer reports on Form 1040 line 4a
Fact.Description: The secondary filer's gross Roth IRA distributions for line 4a: her Part III line 19 plus her qualified distributions with no Part III. Each term is complete-safe, so this is $0 when neither intake is answered. Her taxable Part III amount is carried separately by /spouseForm8606Line25cOrZero to Form 1040 line 4b and the IRA MAGI upper-bound consumer.

Fact.Name: Both filers' Roth IRA distributions for Form 1040 line 4a, beyond what the Form 1099-R route already carries
Fact.Description: For each filer, the Roth gross (/form8606RothGrossDistributions or /spouseForm8606RothGrossDistributions: Part III line 19 plus the qualified Roth distributions that have no Part III) less the box 1 of that filer's Roth IRA Forms 1099-R the Form 1099-R route already totals on line 4a (/primaryFilerRothGrossOnTheForm1099RRoute, /secondaryFilerRothGrossOnTheForm1099RRoute), never below $0; the two filers' results summed. income:/iraDistributions adds this OUTSIDE its route Switch, on the same footing as /form8606Line25cOrZero in income:/taxableIraDistributions: the Part III chain is not gated on /claimsForm8606, so a Roth-only filer selects none of the traditional-IRA routes. A Roth distribution reported on a Form 1099-R in that route and on line 19 is ONE distribution, and line 4a takes the total distribution once (i1040gi Lines 4a and 4b); the larger of the two reports is what reaches line 4a. NOT ADDED TO /form8606GrossDistributions, deliberately: that fact is a Part I/II pro-rata operand, and a Roth term there would corrupt the traditional-IRA worksheet. Complete-safe; $0 on a return that answers neither.

Fact.Name: This Form 1099-R's box 1 is a Roth IRA distribution the Form 1099-R route already puts on Form 1040 line 4a
Fact.Description: Box 1 of this Form 1099-R when box 7 carries a Roth IRA distribution code (form1099RFrontier:../isRothIraDistributionCode) and the form is in the IRA population whose box 1 the Form 1099-R route totals on line 4a (the IRA/SEP/SIMPLE box checked, or a code 8 corrective pair with J or K); $0 otherwise, and $0 while any of those answers is still blank. The same Roth distribution is also on Form 8606 line 19 when Part III is open, so the Part III gross that income:/iraDistributions adds beside the route counts only what is above this amount.

Fact.Name: The primary filer's Roth IRA Form 1099-R box 1 total already on Form 1040 line 4a
Fact.Description: /form1099Rs/*/form8606RothGrossOnTheForm1099RRoute summed over the primary filer's Forms 1099-R, when the Form 1099-R route carries Form 1040 line 4a (form1099Rs:/hasIraDistribution1099R); $0 when that route is not taken or no such form is present.

Fact.Description: /form1099Rs/*/form8606RothGrossOnTheForm1099RRoute summed over the Forms 1099-R not known to be the primary filer's, when the Form 1099-R route carries Form 1040 line 4a; $0 when that route is not taken or no such form is present.

Fact.Name: Made a Roth IRA contribution, conversion or rollover for a year from 1998 through 2020
Fact.Description: Screen "Roth IRA contributions before 2021", in the Form 8606 Part III group. QUESTION: "Did you make a contribution to a Roth IRA -- including a conversion, or a rollover from a qualified retirement plan -- for any year from 1998 through 2020?" HELP: the first-time homebuyer exception to the tax on a Roth distribution is only available once the account has satisfied the 5-year clock of section 408A(d)(2)(B), which for a 2025 distribution means a Roth contribution for some year no later than 2020. The Form 8606 instructions state the test in exactly those words: enter first-time homebuyer expenses on line 20 only "If you had a qualified first-time homebuyer distribution from your Roth IRA and you made a contribution (including a conversion or a rollover from a qualified retirement plan) to a Roth IRA for any year from 1998 through 2020" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i8606.pdf, page 14). ASKED WHEN the filer reports a nonqualified Roth distribution on line 19. UNANSWERED: read as NO. That is not a silent adverse default: it is only consulted when the filer has entered a positive line 20, and in that case the return is REFUSED rather than recomputed, so the filer is told to answer rather than charged for not answering. VALIDATION: yes or no. FEEDS /form8606ClaimsRothContribution1998Through2020 and, through it, /knockoutForm8606FirstTimeHomebuyerWithoutQualifyingRothContribution. Not printed: Form 8606 carries no box for it, and the filer certifies it by entering line 20 at all.

Fact.Name: Roth contribution for a 1998-2020 year, complete-safe
Fact.Description: The 1998-2020 Roth-contribution attestation when answered, else false. The unanswered-false reading is safe here precisely because the only consumer is a REFUSAL: an unanswered attestation beside a positive line 20 blocks submission rather than silently removing the filer's first-time homebuyer reduction, so the filer is asked again instead of being charged.

Fact.Name: Knockout: Form 8606 line 20 entered without a 1998-2020 Roth contribution
Fact.Description: Line 20 reduces the distribution that reaches Form 1040 line 4b dollar for dollar, and i8606 makes the entry conditional on a Roth contribution for a year from 1998 through 2020 -- the section 408A(d)(2)(B) 5-year clock, which a 2025 distribution can only satisfy through a contribution for 2020 or earlier. Nothing on this return derives that history, so the condition is an attestation and the failure mode is a refusal. WHY A REFUSAL AND NOT A ZEROING. Reading the unanswered attestation as "no" and setting line 20 to $0 would take the filer's own entry away silently and raise the tax; refusing tells the filer which question to answer. The residue is permanent and is intake completeness, not arithmetic: a positive line 20 beside an unanswered or negative attestation is a state no derivation can resolve. BLOCKS SUBMISSION AND IS A MEMBER OF flow:/flowIsKnockedOut, like its spouse twin: a user-input-contradiction guard (scope-sidecar revisit_trigger beginning "n/a"), wired to the knockout screen so either filer's Part III refusal is reached the same way. NOT COVERED, and named rather than implied: the $10,000 lifetime cap's REDUCTION by prior qualified first-time homebuyer distributions. That is a lifetime history this single-year graph does not carry. The $10,000 itself needs no history and is enforced as a Max on the intake. Also aggregates the secondary filer's corresponding Part III refusal. Only a positive line 19 opens each filer's line 20 eligibility check.

Fact.Name: Knockout: Form 8606 Part III started and left partly blank
Fact.Description:
A filer who reports a nonqualified Roth distribution on line 19 and leaves a required Part III line blank makes /form8606Line25a Incomplete, and /form8606Line25cOrZero -- which must stay Complete because Form 1040 line 4b reads it -- resolves the whole taxable distribution to $0. This fact refuses that state instead. THE THREE DEFECTS, and only those three. Line 20 blank: the form prints NO skip rule for it, so a filer who answers line 19 and skips line 20 is simply incomplete. Line 22 blank while line 21 is positive: line 22 is unconditional once line 21 is more than zero. Line 24 blank while line 23 is positive: same. Each is an intake-completeness residue with no answer the dictionary can supply, which is why this is a permanent refusal and not a fill. THE TWO BENIGN BLANKS ARE DELIBERATELY NOT REFUSED, and they are why this is an ordered chain rather than one Not(IsComplete(line 25a)) test. The form says "If line 21 is zero, stop here" at line 22 and "If zero or less, enter -0- and skip lines 24 and 25" at line 23, so a blank line 22 behind a zero line 21, and a blank line 24 behind a zero line 23, are the printed instruction being followed. Both leave line 25a Incomplete and both resolve correctly to a $0 line 4b, so refusing them would refuse the form's own directions. THE CHAIN IS ORDERED because each test needs the line above it answered: line 21 is Incomplete until line 20 is answered, and line 23 is Incomplete until line 22 is. Each Case's When is therefore an IsComplete on the intake immediately above, and the GreaterThan that decides between defect and skip rule runs only inside the arm where its operand is known Complete. SILENT FOR EVERY RETURN THAT DOES NOT OPEN PART III: the outermost guard is IsComplete of line 19 itself -- a genuine "the filer answered" predicate on a bare writable, never IsComplete of a complete-safe fact -- and then line 19 greater than zero, which is the printed entry condition (i8606 says a filer with no amount for line 19 must not complete Part III at all and reports the distribution on Form 1040 line 4a instead). BLOCKS SUBMISSION AND IS A MEMBER OF flow:/flowIsKnockedOut, like its spouse twin: a data-completeness guard (scope-sidecar revisit_trigger beginning "n/a"). Also aggregates the secondary filer's corresponding Part III refusal. The former spouse Part III income-integration guard no longer reaches this submission surface: both line 4b and the IRA MAGI upper-bound consumer now read the spouse's complete-safe line 25c export.
Submission-blocking Part III completeness check. A positive line 19 requires line 20; positive line 21 requires the applied line-22 result, and positive line 23 requires line 24. The form's zero-line stop rules remain allowed. Applied line 22 can come from an answered legacy amount or a fully reconciled calculated history. Incomplete/contradictory selected histories cannot be hidden by an answered manual amount. The primary guard retains its existing secondary-filer and non-joint-return checks. No new historical input is required unless its calculator is selected.

Fact.Name: Knockout: a qualified disaster portion exceeds the Form 8606 line it is part of
Fact.Description: Form 8606 line 15b is "the amount on line 15a attributable to qualified disaster distributions" and line 25b is the same words over line 25a, so neither can exceed the line it is a part of. Read from Form 8915-F lines 18 and 19, both can: the two forms are answered independently and nothing else compares them. Refusing is the only honest answer - clamping would silently rewrite the filer's Form 8915-F figure, and letting it stand makes line 15c or line 25c negative and understates Form 1040 line 4b by the excess. THE ROTH ARM IS SWITCH-GUARDED because line 25a is Incomplete on every return that opens no Part III; the traditional arms need no guard because lines 15a and 15b are both complete-safe. Silent for every return that files no Form 8915-F, where both disaster portions are 0 and no line can be exceeded. TWO RESIDUES THIS FACT DOES NOT COVER, named rather than implied. FIRST, the Roth arm is silent whenever line 25a is Incomplete, and that includes the states the form's own skip rules produce - line 21 of zero ("stop here"), and line 23 of zero or less with lines 24 and 25 skipped - so a positive Form 8915-F line 19 against a Part III that stopped is not compared to anything here. It is refused instead by /knockoutForm8606QualifiedDisasterAmountWithoutAForm8606 only when line 19 itself was never answered; a filer who answered line 19, stopped at a printed skip rule and still entered a Form 8915-F line 19 is not refused by either. SECOND, i8606's own fraction bounds line 15b by line 15a times qualified disaster distributions over line 7 (and line 25b by line 25a times the same numerator over line 21), which is TIGHTER than the bound checked here: in i8606's Example 1 the true bound is $20,000 against the $30,000 this fact checks. Fact.Name: Knockout: Form 8915-F sends an amount to a Form 8606 part this return does not file
Fact.Description: Form 8915-F line 17 asks whether the filer received a qualified disaster distribution from an IRA "that is required to be reported on this year's Form 8606", and lines 18 and 19 carry the two figures that Form 8606 lines 15b and 25b hold. A Yes on line 17, or a positive line 18 or 19, therefore asserts that a Form 8606 exists on this return. THE TEST IS PER LINE, not one combined test, because the three answers assert different things. Line 18 IS Form 8606 line 15b, a PART I figure, so a positive line 18 with neither filer claiming Part I is refused even when a Part III is open. Line 19 IS Form 8606 line 25b, a PART III figure, so a positive line 19 with no Part III open is refused even when Part I is claimed. Line 17 asserts only that SOME Form 8606 carries the distribution, so its arm requires that neither Part I nor Part III exists. Combining the three into one test with a shared Not(Part I) AND Not(Part III) conjunct silences both cross cases, which is what this fact did when it first landed. Before the lines 15b/25b wire the contradiction was invisible altogether, because Form 8606 hard-zeroed both boxes and the two modules never met. WHAT THE FILER DOES INSTEAD, and why this is not a scope-out: the answer is to complete the Form 8606 the distribution requires, which this module builds. Line 20 - the qualified disaster amount NOT reported on Form 8606 - is untouched by this guard and is the right line for a distribution that belongs on no Form 8606 at all. the Roth worksheet uses direct repayment subtraction and per-filer Part III attribution; unresolved two-filer disaster attribution remains refused.

Attributing it to the primary would be a silent default that understates one spouse's line 15c and overstates the other's, so the return is refused instead and neither filer's line 15b takes the amount. Fact.Name: Form 8606 line 20 - qualified first-time homebuyer expenses
Fact.Description: Screen "First-time homebuyer expenses paid from your Roth IRA", in the Form 8606 Part III group. QUESTION: "How much of your 2025 Roth IRA distribution did you use for qualified first-time homebuyer expenses?" HELP: qualified first-time homebuyer expenses are the costs of acquiring, constructing or reconstructing a principal residence for a buyer who had no present ownership interest in a principal residence during the two years before the acquisition, paid within 120 days of the distribution. The printed line says "Do not enter more than $10,000 reduced by the total of all your prior qualified first-time homebuyer distributions" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f8606.pdf, page 2): the $10,000 is a LIFETIME aggregate under section 72(t)(8)(B), so if you have used part of it in an earlier year, enter only what is left. ASKED WHEN the filer reports a nonqualified Roth distribution on line 19; it is asked of every such filer, because the form prints no skip rule for it. UNANSWERED: the return is REFUSED (/knockoutForm8606PartIIIPartiallyAnswered), not defaulted -- a blank here makes line 25a Incomplete, and the alternative to refusing is sending the whole taxable distribution to Form 1040 line 4b as $0. Enter 0 if none. VALIDATION: dollars and cents, minimum $0, maximum $10,000 -- the statutory lifetime ceiling, which needs no history. The REDUCTION by prior-year first-time homebuyer distributions is NOT enforced here: it is a lifetime figure this single-year graph does not carry, and the help text asks the filer to apply it. FEEDS Form 8606 line 21 (line 19 minus this) and so lines 23, 25a and 25c, and Form 1040 line 4b -- every dollar entered here reduces the taxable Roth distribution dollar for dollar. Fact.Name: Form 8606 line 10 in thousandths, as the division and rounding nodes first produce it
Fact.Description: 1000 times line 5 divided by line 9, rounded to a whole number of thousandths and capped at 1000, when line 9 is above $0; $0 when line 9 is $0 or less. This is an intermediate figure and not the printed line. A Dollar division is reduced to cents (half to even) before the outer Round takes it to whole thousandths (half up), so a true quotient a fraction of a cent below one half of a thousandth is rounded up; the cent reduction moves a value by at most half a cent, so the only possible error here is one thousandth too high. /form8606Line10Thousandths corrects that step with exact cent arithmetic.

Fact.Name: Form 8606 line 10 decimal times 1000
Fact.Description: Form 8606 line 10, "Divide line 5 by line 9. Enter the result as a decimal rounded to at least 3 places. If the result is 1.000 or more, enter 1.000", carried as INTEGER THOUSANDTHS so the third decimal place the printed line demands is exact: line 10 times 1000. The numerator is /form8606Line5 (total basis in traditional IRAs for 2025, the printed line 5) and the denominator is /form8606Line9 (the printed line 9, the value of all traditional IRAs plus distributions plus conversions). MULTIPLY FIRST, DIVIDE LAST: scaling by 1000 before the divide keeps the third decimal place, which a Dollar quotient taken at two places would already have lost. The printed 1.000 ceiling is the LesserOf against 1000, and the complete safe 0 arm covers the line 9 of zero the pro rata rule cannot divide by. CONSUMED BY THE PRO RATA LINES: /form8606NontaxableConversionPortion and /form8606NontaxableDistributionPortion, the printed lines 11 and 12, MULTIPLY BY THIS RATIO and divide by 1000 rather than recomputing line 5 / line 9 at full precision. That is what makes the printed Part I foot to its own arithmetic: line 11 is "Multiply line 8 by line 10" and line 12 is "Multiply line 7 by line 10", and line 10 is the three-decimal number this fact prints. ONE RATIO PER FILER. The secondary filer's printed lines 11 and 12 read her own /spouseForm8606Line10Thousandths the same way, so each filer's printed Part I foots to its own printed line 10. /form8606Ws11NontaxablePortion answers line 5 over line 9 exactly instead; that is compliant, because both the form and the publication say "rounded to at least 3 places" (f8606:57-58, p590b:1188-1189), and Worksheet 1-1 is never printed, so it has no printed line 10 to foot to. AN UNANSWERED PART I STAYS UNANSWERED. The divide arm and the 0 arm are mutually exclusive on line 9: the 0 arm is taken only when line 9 is known to be zero or less. While line 9 is itself unknown, because line 6, 7 or 8 is left blank, this fact is Incomplete rather than 0, so lines 11 and 12 and every total built on them stay Incomplete instead of carrying a figure computed from a ratio the filer has not supplied. THE PRIMARY FILER'S COPY: the register renders one Form 8606 per item of /filersRequiredToFileForm8606, and /filers/*/form8606PrintedLine10Thousandths picks this fact on the primary filer's copy and /spouseForm8606Line10Thousandths on the secondary filer's. The printed decimal is ONE half-up rounding of the true quotient: this fact starts from /form8606Line10RoundedAfterCentSnap and steps it down by one thousandth exactly when 2,000 times line 5 is less than (2 times that figure minus 1) times line 9, the exact cent comparison saying the true quotient is below the lower half-thousandth boundary. Every product in that comparison is a whole number of cents, so no rounding enters the test.
